position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and hobby farming, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering and brand reputation. Begin with a limited pilot to test demand and willingness to pay before full-scale rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer‑focused products.
Evidence must justify investment; financial data is unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming).
2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a new product proposition.
3) No expansion: continue current business model with independent dealers and existing product line.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop and market a consumer‑focused product.

T1.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, time-saving solution for small-scale landscaping or hobby farming, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company gains higher margins and brand equity by selling directly to consumers and capturing design control.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers in 1962 value efficiency and reliability; a tractor engineered for light use (e.g., mowing, snow blowing) addresses their need for a single, versatile tool, reducing the need for multiple equipment purchases.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells through its own retail channels, retaining control over pricing and branding, and can command premium prices justified by brand reputation and product differentiation.
assumptions: Consumers in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to purchase a lawn tractor.
Deere can produce a differentiated model that meets consumer expectations for performance and safety.
Independent dealers will continue to distribute the product effectively.
predictions: If a test offers a consumer-focused lawn tractor at a price 15% above a comparable competitor, purchase intent will be at least 20% higher among target consumers.
Surveyed consumers will rank Deere as the most trusted brand for small-scale landscaping when presented with a differentiated proposition.
T1.first_claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a convenient, time-saving solution for small-scale landscaping or hobby farming, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand they trust.

T2.claim: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive the product as a status symbol reflecting modern lifestyle and home improvement, and are willing to pay a premium for brand prestige.
T2.who_benefits: Deere & Company gains higher margins and brand equity by selling directly to consumers and leveraging its established reputation as a premium agricultural brand.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: In 1962, home ownership and suburban growth increase demand for tools that signal modernity and success. A lawn tractor marketed as a status item (e.g., equipped with advanced features, branded with Deere's heritage) would attract consumers
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere sells through its own retail channels, retaining control over pricing and branding, and can command premium prices justified by brand reputation and product differentiation.
assumptions: Consumers in 1962 associate Deere with quality and reliability, making the brand a status signal.
A differentiated proposition can be positioned as a lifestyle product rather than a utilitarian tool.
Independent dealers will continue to distribute the product effectively.
predictions: If a test offers a consumer-focused lawn tractor priced 20% above a comparable competitor, purchase intent will be at least 15% higher among consumers who value status.
Surveyed consumers will rank Deere as the most prestigious brand for home improvement when presented with a differentiated proposition.

X1.name: Consumer Messaging Test: Status vs. Convenience
X1.method: Online controlled experiment with two landing pages for a simulated consumer lawn tractor. Participants view one page emphasizing convenience and time-saving benefits (status neutral), and the other page emphasizing status and modern lifestyle appeal (status driven). After viewing, participants indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑ "not interested" to 7‑ "very interested").
X1.sample: 500 U.S. adults recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported interest in home improvement. Randomly assigned to either status page or convenience page.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑ to 7) for participants who see the corresponding page.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants viewing the convenience page will have a mean score ≥ 5.0 (indicating at least 5% higher intent than the status page).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants viewing the status page will have a mean score ≥ 5.0 (indicating at least 5% higher intent than the convenience page).

X1.decision_rule: If the difference in mean scores between the two groups is ≥ 0.5 points, proceed with the differentiated proposition aligned with the higher‑score page. If the difference is ≤ 0.5 points, the proposition should be developed only if the status page yields a ≥ 0.5 point advantage.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns a label printer reducing packing errors and does not address consumer demand, status perception, or willingness to pay for a differentiated proposition. Therefore it does not affect T1.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale landscaping and hobby farming, leveraging Deere’s tractor engineering. Begin with a limited pilot of a utility‑focused lawn tractor sold through independent dealers, using the proposed test to validate demand before scaling.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeframe for any proposed experiment.
Must assess current reach to individual buyers and market demand for consumer‑focused products.
Evidence must justify investment; financial data is unavailable.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑scale landscaping, hobby farming).
2) Expand existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a new product proposition.
3) No expansion: continue current business model with independent dealers and existing product line.
4) License tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Partner with consumer brands to co‑develop and market a consumer‑focused product.

X1.method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized messaging. Participants view two product concepts: a utility lawn tractor (engineered for small-scale landscaping, price comparable to competitors) and a status lawn tractor (same engineering, priced 10% above, marketed as a modern lifestyle item). Participants indicate which concept they would purchase and justify their choice.
X1.sample: 200 U.S. adults aged 25-55, recruited via an online panel, balanced for gender and home ownership status (owner vs non-owner). Stratify by self-reported interest in home improvement (high vs low).
X1.measure: Primary outcome: binary choice (utilities vs status). Secondary: willingness-to-pay (WTP) difference between the two concepts.

arguments.name: Consumer Proposition Test: Utility vs Status Messaging

Participants view two product concepts: a utility lawn tractor (engineered for small-scale landscaping, price comparable to competitors) and a status lawn tractor (same engineering, priced 10% above, marketed as a modern lifestyle item). Participants indicate which concept they would purchase and justify their choice.

arguments.measure: Primary outcome: binary choice (utilities vs status). Secondary: willingness-to-pay (WTP) difference between the two concepts.
